entries.1:1: This opens the story of Jesus by tracing his family line back to King David and to Abraham, the father of the Jewish people. It tells the reader that Jesus stands in a long, promised family history, not out of nowhere.
entries.1:2: The family line moves from Abraham to Isaac to Jacob and then to Judah and his brothers. It shows God's promises being passed down through real, ordinary generations of a family.
entries.1:3: The line continues through Judah and his sons, including Perez, whose mother was Tamar. It reminds the reader that Jesus' ancestors included messy family situations, not just tidy ones.
entries.1:4: The generations keep going, from Ram to Amminadab to Nahshon to Salmon. Each name is a link in the chain that leads to Jesus.
entries.1:5: This part of the line includes Rahab and Ruth, two women from outside Israel's main family. It shows that Jesus' family story already included outsiders and surprises.
entries.1:6: The line reaches King David and then Solomon, whose mother was Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah. It honestly names a painful episode in the family, showing Jesus came from real people with real failures.
entries.1:7: The royal line continues through Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, and Asa. These were kings of Judah, and their names show Jesus' connection to Israel's throne.
entries.1:8: The family line goes on through Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Uzziah. It keeps the reader moving through history toward Jesus.
entries.1:9: The line passes through Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Some of these kings were faithful and some were not, yet God's plan kept moving forward.
entries.1:10: The generations continue through Manasseh, Amon, and Josiah. This shows that even through flawed kings, the family line leading to Jesus was preserved.
entries.1:11: Josiah's sons lived at the time when Judah was taken away to Babylon. This marks a low point of exile in Jesus' family history.
entries.1:12: After the exile, the line continues through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. It shows that God's plan did not stop when his people were defeated and taken away.
entries.1:13: The family line carries on through Abiud, Eliakim, and Azor. These are less famous names, but they matter because they keep the chain unbroken.
entries.1:14: The generations continue through Zadok, Achim, and Eliud. Ordinary names like these show that Jesus' coming was prepared over many quiet years.
entries.1:15: The line moves through Eleazar and Matthan to Jacob. Each step brings the family story closer to Jesus' birth.
entries.1:16: Jacob was the father of Joseph, who was the husband of Mary, and Mary gave birth to Jesus, called the Christ. This is the point of the whole list: it leads to Jesus.
entries.1:17: Matthew sums up the family line in three groups of fourteen generations. The pattern helps the reader see that history was moving in an ordered way toward Jesus.
entries.1:18: Jesus' birth happened like this: Mary was promised to Joseph, but before they lived together she was found to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit. This tells the reader that Jesus' birth was God's doing, not an ordinary human event.
entries.1:19: Joseph was a good man and did not want to shame Mary publicly, so he planned to end the engagement quietly. It shows Joseph's kindness even in a confusing and painful situation.
entries.1:20: While Joseph was thinking about this, an angel spoke to him in a dream and told him not to be afraid to marry Mary, because her child was from the Holy Spirit. It tells the reader that God guided Joseph through his doubts.
entries.1:21: The angel said Mary would have a son named Jesus, because he would save his people from their sins. The name itself points to the purpose of his life.
entries.1:22: All this happened to fulfill what God had spoken through a prophet long before. It tells the reader that Jesus' birth was part of God's plan, not an accident.
entries.1:23: The prophet said a virgin would have a son called Immanuel, which means God with us. This tells the reader that in Jesus, God came near to people.
entries.1:24: Joseph woke up and did what the angel told him, taking Mary as his wife. It shows Joseph trusting and obeying God even when it was costly.
entries.1:25: Joseph did not live with Mary as husband and wife until after she gave birth, and he named the baby Jesus. It confirms that Jesus was born of Mary as the angel had said.
entries.2:1: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem during King Herod's reign, visitors from eastern lands arrived in Jerusalem. It shows that people far away were drawn to seek Jesus, and it invites the reader to seek him too.
entries.2:2: The visitors asked where the newborn king of the Jews was, because they had seen his star and came to honor him. It shows that Jesus deserves worship, and the reader is invited to honor him as well.
entries.2:3: When King Herod heard about this, he and the whole city of Jerusalem were disturbed. It shows that news of Jesus can unsettle people in power, and it reminds the reader that Jesus' kingship challenges other loyalties.
entries.2:4: Herod gathered the religious leaders and asked them where the Messiah was to be born. It shows that knowing the facts about God's promises is not the same as welcoming the one they point to.
entries.2:5: They answered that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem, as the prophet had written. It shows God keeps his promises, and the reader can trust what he has said.
entries.2:6: The prophecy says Bethlehem, though small, would produce a ruler who would shepherd God's people. It shows God often works through the small and humble, and it points to Jesus as that shepherd.
entries.2:7: Herod secretly met the visitors and asked exactly when the star had appeared. It shows Herod was scheming, and it warns the reader that not everyone who asks about Jesus has good intentions.
entries.2:8: Herod sent them to Bethlehem and asked them to report back so he could worship the child too, though he was lying. It shows that false words can hide harmful plans, and the reader should be wise about motives.
entries.2:9: The visitors left, and the star they had seen led them until it stopped over the place where the child was. It shows God guided them to Jesus, and the reader can trust God to lead them to him too.
entries.2:10: Seeing the star again filled them with great joy. It shows that finding Jesus brings real joy, and the reader can expect joy in seeking him.
entries.2:11: They entered the house, saw the child with Mary, bowed down and worshiped him, and gave him gold, incense, and spices. It shows Jesus is worthy of worship and costly gifts, and the reader is invited to give him their best.
entries.2:12: God warned them in a dream not to return to Herod, so they went home by a different route. It shows God protects those who follow him, and the reader can trust his guidance even when plans change.
entries.2:13: An angel told Joseph in a dream to take the child and Mary to Egypt because Herod wanted to kill him. It shows God warns and protects his people, and the reader can trust God's care in danger.
entries.2:14: Joseph got up at once and took the child and his mother to Egypt during the night. It shows Joseph obeyed quickly, and the reader is encouraged to act on God's direction without delay.
entries.2:15: They stayed in Egypt until Herod died, fulfilling the prophet's words about God calling his son out of Egypt. It shows God's plans come true even through hardship, and the reader can trust his word.
entries.2:16: Herod was furious when the visitors did not return, so he had all the boys two years old and under in Bethlehem and the area killed. It shows the terrible cost of rejecting Jesus, and the reader sees how far human evil can go.
entries.2:17: This fulfilled what the prophet Jeremiah had spoken. It shows God's word stands even in tragedy, and the reader can trust that Scripture is reliable.
entries.2:18: The prophecy describes loud weeping in Ramah, Rachel crying for her children and refusing comfort. It shows God does not ignore grief, and the reader can bring deep sorrow honestly before him.
entries.2:19: After Herod died, an angel came to Joseph in a dream while he was in Egypt. It shows God knows when the danger has passed, and the reader can trust his timing.
entries.2:20: The angel told Joseph to take the child and Mary back to Israel because those who wanted to kill the child were dead. It shows God brings his people safely through danger, and the reader can trust his protection.
entries.2:21: Joseph got up and took the child and his mother back to the land of Israel. It shows Joseph kept obeying God step by step, and the reader is encouraged to do the same.
entries.2:22: When Joseph heard that Archelaus was ruling in place of his father Herod, he was afraid, and after a dream warning he went to the region of Galilee. It shows God guides through real fears, and the reader can trust his direction in uncertain situations.
entries.2:23: Joseph settled in a town called Nazareth, fulfilling what the prophets said about the Messiah being called a Nazarene. It shows God's plan unfolds in ordinary places, and the reader sees that Jesus' humble background was part of God's purpose.
entries.3:1: John the Baptist began preaching in the desert region of Judea. This shows that God sometimes starts His work in unlikely, out-of-the-way places.
entries.3:2: John told people to turn away from their sins because God's kingdom was coming near. The reader is also called to change direction and take God's rule seriously.
entries.3:3: John was the messenger Isaiah had predicted, the one calling people to prepare for the Lord's coming. It reminds us that God announces His plans ahead of time through His messengers.
entries.3:4: John dressed and ate very simply, like an old-time prophet. His lifestyle shows that his message mattered more to him than comfort or appearances.
entries.3:5: Crowds from Jerusalem and the whole region came out to hear John. People are drawn to a message that is honest about sin and calls for real change.
entries.3:6: People were baptized in the Jordan River while openly admitting their wrongs. Confessing sin honestly is the first step toward a changed life.
entries.3:7: John sharply warned the religious leaders who came, calling them a brood of snakes and asking who had warned them to flee coming judgment. Being religious on the outside does not protect anyone from God's judgment.
entries.3:8: John told them to prove their repentance by the way they lived. Real sorrow for sin shows up in changed actions, not just words.
entries.3:9: John warned them not to rely on being Abraham's descendants, since God could raise up children for Abraham from stones. Family background or religious heritage cannot replace personal faith and obedience.
entries.3:10: John pictured judgment as an axe already laid at the root of the trees, with fruitless trees cut down and burned. A life that produces no good fruit faces serious consequences.
entries.3:11: John baptized with water for repentance, but he pointed to a greater one coming after him who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. John's baptism was only preparation for the greater work Jesus would do.
entries.3:12: John described the coming one as a farmer who separates good grain from chaff, storing the grain and burning the useless chaff with unquenchable fire. Jesus will sort out what is genuine from what is worthless.
entries.3:13: Jesus traveled from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. Even though He had no sin, Jesus chose to identify with the people He came to save.
entries.3:14: John tried to stop Jesus, feeling that he himself needed baptism from Jesus instead. It is fitting to feel unworthy before Jesus, yet He humbly comes to us anyway.
entries.3:15: Jesus told John to allow it for now, because it was right to fulfill all righteousness. Jesus did what was right even when it seemed unnecessary, showing His obedience to God's plan.
entries.3:16: As Jesus came up from the water, the heavens opened and He saw God's Spirit descend on Him like a dove. This marks Jesus as the one empowered and chosen by God for His mission.
entries.3:17: A voice from heaven declared that Jesus is God's beloved Son, in whom He is well pleased. God the Father openly affirmed His Son, showing that Jesus is exactly who He claimed to be.
entries.4:1: God's Spirit led Jesus into a lonely desert place so he would be tested by the devil. God may allow hard times to test us, but he is still guiding us through them.
entries.4:2: Jesus fasted from food for forty days and nights, and by the end he was very hungry. His testing came when he was at his weakest, which reminds us that temptation often hits us when we are worn down.
entries.4:3: The devil challenged Jesus to prove who he was by turning stones into bread. He tempted him to use his power for his own comfort instead of trusting God.
entries.4:4: Jesus answered that people need more than food to live; they need every word God speaks. Physical things keep us alive, but God's word feeds our souls, so we should treasure it.
entries.4:5: The devil took Jesus to Jerusalem and stood him on the highest part of the Temple. He kept pushing Jesus to test God's care in dramatic ways.
entries.4:6: The devil quoted Scripture to urge Jesus to jump, claiming angels would catch him. He twisted God's words to tempt Jesus into showing off and forcing God to prove himself.
entries.4:7: Jesus replied that we must not test the Lord our God. Trusting God does not mean daring him to prove himself; it means obeying him without demanding signs.
entries.4:8: The devil showed Jesus all the world's kingdoms and their splendor from a high mountain. He offered a shortcut to power and glory instead of God's way.
entries.4:9: The devil promised to give Jesus all these kingdoms if he would bow down and worship him. He wanted Jesus to take the easy road by giving him the honor that belongs to God alone.
entries.4:10: Jesus told Satan to get away and said we must worship and serve only the Lord God. No shortcut or prize is worth giving our ultimate loyalty to anything other than God.
entries.4:11: The devil left Jesus, and angels came to care for him. When we resist temptation, God does not abandon us; he strengthens and comforts us afterward.
entries.4:12: When Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been put in prison, he withdrew to Galilee. He continued his mission even when danger was closing in around him.
entries.4:13: Jesus left Nazareth and made his home in Capernaum by the sea. He chose a busy lakeside town as the base for his ministry.
entries.4:14: This move happened so that what the prophet Isaiah had said long before would come true. God's plans spoken through the prophets are fulfilled in Jesus.
entries.4:15: Isaiah named the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, near the sea and across the Jordan, as Galilee where many non-Jews lived. God's light was coming to a region often overlooked.
entries.4:16: People living in darkness saw a great light, and dawn broke for those in the shadow of death. Jesus brings hope and life to those who feel lost and hopeless.
entries.4:17: From then on Jesus preached that people should turn from their sin because the kingdom of heaven was near. God's rule was breaking in, and people needed to change their hearts and lives.
entries.4:18: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, casting a net because they were fishermen. He came to ordinary working people, not just religious leaders.
entries.4:19: Jesus told them to follow him, and he would make them fishers of people. Following Jesus means he will use our everyday skills to help others find him.
entries.4:21: Jesus saw two more brothers, James and John, in a boat with their father mending nets, and he called them. He invites people right in the middle of their daily work.
entries.4:22: They left the boat and their father at once and followed Jesus. Following him can mean leaving behind even family and familiar work when he calls.
entries.4:23: Jesus traveled through Galilee teaching in synagogues, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every kind of sickness. He cared for both people's souls and their bodies.
entries.4:24: News about Jesus spread through Syria, and people brought him the sick, the troubled, and the paralyzed, and he healed them all. His compassion reached beyond his own people to anyone in need.
entries.4:25: Large crowds from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and across the Jordan followed him. People came from everywhere because they saw and heard what he could do.
entries.5:1: Jesus saw a large crowd, so he went up a mountain and sat down, and his disciples gathered around him to listen. It shows he wanted to teach his closest followers in a quiet place apart from the crowd.
entries.5:2: Jesus began to speak and teach them. This simply introduces the famous teaching that follows.
entries.5:3: People who know they are spiritually needy and depend on God are truly blessed, because God's kingdom belongs to them. It means real happiness starts with humility, not self-confidence.
entries.5:4: Those who are grieving or sad are blessed because God will comfort them. It means your sorrow is not the end, and God promises to bring you relief.
entries.5:5: Gentle, humble people who don't push others around are blessed because they will inherit the earth. It means quiet strength, not aggression, is what God rewards.
entries.5:6: Those who deeply hunger and thirst to do what is right are blessed because that desire will be satisfied. It means God honors a genuine longing to live rightly.
entries.5:7: Those who show mercy and kindness to others are blessed because they will receive mercy. It means the way you treat others comes back to you in God's dealings with you.
entries.5:8: People with pure, sincere hearts are blessed because they will see God. It means inner honesty and cleanliness matter more than outward appearance.
entries.5:9: Those who work to make peace are blessed and will be called God's children. It means peacemaking is a family trait of God's people.
entries.5:10: Those who are mistreated because they do what is right are blessed, because God's kingdom belongs to them. It means suffering for goodness does not mean you have lost God's favor.
entries.5:11: You are blessed when people insult you, treat you badly, or lie about you because you follow Jesus. It means rejection for his sake is not a sign of failure.
entries.5:12: Rejoice, because your reward in heaven is great, just as the prophets before you were also mistreated. It means present trouble is small compared to what God has promised.
entries.5:13: You are like salt that preserves and flavors the world, but salt that loses its taste is useless. It means your faith should make a real difference, or it accomplishes nothing.
entries.5:14: You are like light for the whole world, and a city on a hill cannot be hidden. It means your life should be visible and show others what is good.
entries.5:15: No one lights a lamp and hides it under a bowl; they put it where it gives light to everyone in the house. It means don't hide the good you can do; let it help others.
entries.5:16: Good works are meant to point upward, not inward. Let people see your life and give God the credit.
entries.5:17: Don't think Jesus came to cancel the law or the prophets; he came to fulfill and complete them. It means he takes God's earlier teaching seriously and brings it to its full meaning.
entries.5:18: Not the smallest detail of the law will pass away until everything is accomplished. It means God's word is reliable down to the smallest part.
entries.5:19: Anyone who breaks even the smallest command and teaches others to do the same will be least in God's kingdom, but whoever practices and teaches them will be great. It means both doing and teaching God's word matter.
entries.5:20: Unless your right living goes beyond that of the religious experts of the day, you cannot enter God's kingdom. It means outward rule-keeping alone is not enough; the heart must be changed.
entries.5:21: You have heard the old command not to murder and that murderers face judgment. Jesus is starting to compare the old teaching with his deeper standard.
entries.5:22: Jesus says even anger and insulting words bring you under judgment, with serious consequences. It means God cares about your heart and words, not just your actions.
entries.5:23: If you are bringing an offering to God and remember that someone has something against you, stop. It means broken relationships matter to God even during worship.
entries.5:24: Leave your offering, go make peace with that person first, then come back and give your gift. It means settling conflict with others takes priority over religious ritual.
entries.5:25: Settle disputes with your accuser quickly before it goes to court and you end up in prison. It means deal with conflict early before it gets worse.
entries.5:26: You won't get out until you have paid the last small coin. It means unresolved debts and disputes have real consequences, so take them seriously.
entries.5:27: You have heard the old command not to commit adultery. Jesus is again setting up a deeper point about God's standard.
entries.5:28: Jesus says looking at someone with lustful desire is already adultery in the heart. It means God judges the inner intention, not just the outward act.
entries.5:29: If your eye leads you to sin, it is better to lose it than for your whole body to be destroyed. Jesus uses strong picture language to say: deal ruthlessly with whatever pulls you into sin.
entries.5:30: If your hand causes you to sin, it is better to lose it than for your whole body to be destroyed. It means take sin seriously enough to cut off what leads you into it.
entries.5:31: It was said that a man who divorces his wife must give her a written certificate. Jesus is about to address what that practice really meant.
entries.5:32: Jesus says divorcing your wife for any reason except sexual unfaithfulness makes her an adulteress, and whoever marries her commits adultery too. It means marriage is meant to be taken far more seriously than a casual exit.
entries.5:33: You have heard the old teaching not to swear falsely but to keep your oaths to the Lord. Jesus is about to raise the standard on honesty.
entries.5:34: Jesus says don't swear oaths at all, not by heaven, since heaven is God's throne. It means don't use impressive-sounding vows to make your words seem more reliable.
entries.5:35: Don't swear by the earth, by Jerusalem, or similar things, because they all belong to God. It means everything you might swear by is ultimately God's, so such oaths are empty.
entries.5:36: You can't even swear by your own head, because you can't make a single hair white or black. It means you don't control enough to guarantee anything by an oath.
entries.5:37: Let your yes mean yes and your no mean no; anything beyond that comes from evil. It means simply tell the truth, and your word will be trusted without extra promises.
entries.5:38: You have heard the old rule of an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Jesus is about to challenge the idea of getting even.
entries.5:39: Jesus says don't fight back against an evil person; if someone slaps your right cheek, offer the other too. It means refuse revenge and respond with surprising generosity.
entries.5:40: If someone sues you and takes your coat, let him have your cloak as well. It means don't cling to your rights in a way that feeds conflict.
entries.5:41: If someone forces you to go one mile, go two. It means go beyond what is demanded and respond with willing generosity instead of resentment.
entries.5:42: When someone asks you for help, give it, and don't turn away a person who wants to borrow something from you. This means being generous with what you have rather than holding back.
entries.5:43: People had been taught to love their neighbor but to hate their enemies. Jesus is pointing out the old teaching before he corrects it.
entries.5:44: Jesus tells us to love the people who oppose us and pray for those who treat us badly. This is a hard command, but it shows real love instead of revenge.
entries.5:45: By loving even your enemies you show that you belong to God, who gives sun and rain to both good and bad people. God is kind to everyone, and he wants his children to be like him.
entries.5:46: If you only love people who love you back, there is nothing special about that, since even dishonest people do the same. Real love goes beyond what comes naturally.
entries.5:47: If you only greet your own friends, you are doing nothing more than anyone else does. Jesus wants his followers to treat outsiders with kindness too.
entries.5:48: Jesus calls us to be fully good and mature, just as God our Father is perfect. We won't reach this on our own, but it is the goal he sets for us to grow toward.
entries.6:1: Jesus warns that doing good things just to be noticed by people means that's all the reward you'll get. If you want God's reward, do good for him rather than for an audience.
entries.6:2: Don't announce your charity like show-offs do to win praise. If applause from people is all you're after, that's the only reward you'll receive.
entries.6:3: Give so quietly that even your other hand doesn't know what you're doing. In other words, don't draw attention to your generosity.
entries.6:4: Give secretly, and God, who sees what no one else sees, will reward you. Your giving is between you and him.
entries.6:5: Don't pray in public just to be seen and admired like the show-offs do. If being noticed is your goal, that's all the reward you'll get.
entries.6:6: Pray alone with the door shut, and God, who sees what is secret, will reward you. Honest prayer is directed to God, not performed for people.
entries.6:7: Don't pile up empty words in prayer, thinking God will listen because you talk a lot. More words don't make a better prayer.
entries.6:8: Don't pray like people who don't know God, because your Father already knows what you need before you ask. You can come to him simply and honestly.
entries.6:9: Pray like this: address God as your Father in heaven and treat his name as holy. Prayer starts with who God is, not with what you want.
entries.6:10: Ask for God's kingdom to come and for his will to be done on earth just as it is in heaven. You're asking for God's rule to shape real life here and now.
entries.6:11: Ask God for the bread you need today. It's a simple request for daily provision, trusting him for what you need now.
entries.6:12: Ask God to forgive your debts, just as you forgive those who owe you. Receiving God's forgiveness goes together with forgiving others.
entries.6:13: Ask God not to lead you into testing but to keep you safe from the Evil One. You're asking for protection in the face of temptation and evil.
entries.6:14: If you forgive others when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive you. Forgiveness you receive is tied to forgiveness you give.
entries.6:15: If you refuse to forgive others, you won't receive forgiveness from your Father either. Holding grudges blocks the forgiveness you need.
entries.6:16: When you fast, don't look gloomy like the show-offs who want people to notice. If being seen is your aim, that's all the reward you'll get.
entries.6:17: When you fast, wash your face and look normal. Don't make your fasting a public display.
entries.6:18: Fast without letting anyone see it except your Father, who sees in secret. He will reward you, and your fasting stays between you and him.
entries.6:19: Don't pile up wealth here on earth, where it wears out and thieves can steal it. Earthly treasure doesn't last.
entries.6:20: Store up treasure in heaven, where nothing wears out and no thief can take it. Invest in what lasts forever.
entries.6:21: Your heart follows your treasure, so where you put your wealth shows what you really care about. What you value most will shape your life.
entries.6:22: Your eye is like a lamp for your body; if it's healthy, your whole body is full of light. A clear, honest focus lets light into your whole life.
entries.6:23: If your eye is bad, your whole body is dark, and that darkness is serious. A twisted focus leaves you in deep darkness.
entries.6:24: No one can serve two masters; you'll end up devoted to one and despising the other. You can't give your life to God and to money at the same time.
entries.6:25: Don't be consumed with worry about food, drink, or clothing, because life is more than these things. Worry about basics can crowd out trust in God.
entries.6:26: Look at the birds: they don't plant or store grain, yet your Father feeds them, and you matter far more than they do. If God cares for birds, he'll care for you.
entries.6:27: Worrying can't add even a small amount to your height or your life. Anxiety doesn't actually fix anything.
entries.6:28: Why worry about clothes? Look at how the wild flowers grow without working or making thread. God's care shows in ordinary things.
entries.6:29: Even Solomon in all his splendor wasn't dressed as beautifully as these flowers. God's simple provision outshines human wealth.
entries.6:30: If God clothes grass that's here today and gone tomorrow, he'll surely clothe you, even when your faith is small. You can trust his care.
entries.6:31: Don't run your life by anxious questions about what you'll eat, drink, or wear. Don't let worry set your agenda.
entries.6:32: People who don't know God chase after all these things, but your Father in heaven already knows you need them. You don't have to chase them in panic.
entries.6:33: Put God's kingdom first and the rest finds its place. Anxiety shrinks when the order is right.
entries.6:34: Tomorrow has enough trouble of its own. Today's grace is given for today.
entries.7:1: Jesus tells us not to set ourselves up as judges of other people. If we make a habit of condemning others, we can expect to be judged by the same standard ourselves.
entries.7:2: The way you judge others is the way you will be judged, and the strictness you use on them will be used on you. It is a warning to be fair and merciful rather than harsh.
entries.7:3: It is silly to notice a tiny speck in someone else's eye while ignoring the big plank in your own. We often spot small faults in others while missing our own much bigger ones.
entries.7:4: You cannot offer to help someone with their small problem while your own big problem is still there. Trying to fix others before facing yourself makes you look foolish.
entries.7:5: Jesus calls this person a hypocrite and says to deal with your own fault first. Only then can you see clearly enough to genuinely help someone else.
entries.7:6: Some things are too precious to throw at people who will only trample them and turn on you. Be wise about when and with whom you share what is sacred.
entries.7:7: Ask, seek, knock: prayer is meant to keep going. God is not annoyed by persistence.
entries.7:8: Everyone who asks receives, everyone who seeks finds, and everyone who knocks finds the door opened. God encourages us to keep coming to him in prayer with confidence.
entries.7:9: No normal father would hand his son a stone when the boy asks for bread. Jesus points to ordinary parents to show how reasonable it is to expect good things from God.
entries.7:10: No father would give his son a snake when he asks for a fish. God is not out to trick or harm those who come to him.
entries.7:11: Even imperfect parents know how to give good gifts to their children, so God, who is perfectly good, will surely give good things to those who ask him. You can trust him with your requests.
entries.7:12: Treat others the way you would want them to treat you; this sums up what the law and the prophets teach. It is a simple rule to measure your actions by.
entries.7:13: Enter through the narrow gate, because the easy, wide road leads to ruin and many take it. Following Jesus takes effort and a deliberate choice.
entries.7:14: The gate and road that lead to life are narrow and hard, and few find them. Real life with God costs something and is not the popular path.
entries.7:15: Watch out for false teachers who look harmless like sheep but are dangerous like wolves inside. Judge teachers by what they really are, not by how they appear.
entries.7:16: You can tell what people are really like by what their lives produce, just as you don't pick grapes from thorn bushes. Look at the fruit, not just the words.
entries.7:17: A healthy tree produces good fruit, and a diseased tree produces bad fruit. What is inside a person eventually shows in their actions.
entries.7:18: A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot produce good fruit. The kind of person you are determines the kind of fruit your life bears.
entries.7:19: Any tree that doesn't produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Fruitless or bad living leads to judgment.
entries.7:20: So you will recognize people by the fruit their lives produce. Pay attention to consistent behavior, not just claims.
entries.7:21: Saying 'Lord, Lord' isn't enough to enter heaven; what matters is actually doing what God wants. Words of faith must be backed by obedient living.
entries.7:22: Many will point to their impressive religious activities on judgment day, claiming they did great things in Jesus' name. Even spectacular works are no substitute for truly knowing him.
entries.7:23: Jesus will tell such people plainly that he never knew them and to depart as workers of evil. A close relationship with him matters more than religious performance.
entries.7:24: Anyone who hears Jesus' words and actually puts them into practice is like a wise builder who set his house on solid rock. Hearing is not enough; doing is what makes you secure.
entries.7:25: The storm came and beat against that house, but it stood firm because its foundation was rock. A life built on obeying Jesus can withstand hard times.
entries.7:26: Anyone who hears Jesus' words but doesn't do them is like a foolish builder who put his house on sand. Knowing the right thing without living it leaves you unstable.
entries.7:27: The storm hit that house and it collapsed with a great crash. A life without a solid foundation in doing Jesus' words will not survive the pressures that come.
entries.7:28: When Jesus finished this teaching, the crowds were amazed. His words were striking enough to make people stop and take notice.
entries.7:29: Jesus taught with real authority of his own, unlike the scribes who quoted other teachers. He spoke as someone who had the right to say what he said, so his words deserve our attention.
entries.8:1: A large crowd followed Jesus as he came down from the mountain where he had been teaching. People were drawn to him, and his teaching and healing drew them in close.
entries.8:2: A man with a serious skin disease came and knelt before Jesus, saying that Jesus could heal him if he wanted to. He trusted Jesus' power but left the choice to him.
entries.8:3: Jesus touched the man and said he was willing, and the disease left immediately. Jesus is not distant from people others avoid, and his willingness matters as much as his power.
entries.8:4: Jesus told the man not to tell anyone but to show himself to the priest and give the offering Moses required. This followed the law and gave official proof that he was healed.
entries.8:5: When Jesus entered the town of Capernaum, a Roman army officer came to him asking for help. Even a man of authority and status humbled himself to ask Jesus for something.
entries.8:6: The officer explained that his servant was lying at home paralyzed and suffering terribly. He cared enough about a servant to seek help from Jesus.
entries.8:7: Jesus simply said he would come and heal the servant. He was ready to go to the man's home without hesitation.
entries.8:8: The officer said he did not feel worthy to have Jesus under his roof, and asked Jesus to just say the word and his servant would be healed. He believed Jesus could heal from a distance with only a command.
entries.8:9: The officer explained that he himself was under authority and had soldiers under him who obeyed his orders instantly. He understood that Jesus, too, had authority and that his word alone was enough.
entries.8:10: Jesus was amazed and told the crowd that he had not found faith this strong even among his own people. Faith can show up in unexpected people, and Jesus notices it.
entries.8:11: Jesus said many people would come from far away and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in God's kingdom. People from outside can share fully in God's promises.
entries.8:12: Those who expected to belong by birth would be thrown out into darkness where there is grief and pain. Being an insider by background does not guarantee a place with God.
entries.8:13: Jesus told the officer to go home, and his servant was healed at that very moment because of his faith. Jesus honors trust in him, even from a distance.
entries.8:14: Jesus went into Peter's house and saw Peter's mother-in-law lying in bed with a fever. He noticed the sickness of an ordinary family member and cared about it.
entries.8:15: Jesus touched her hand, the fever left, and she got up and served him. Healing restored her strength and moved her to practical service.
entries.8:16: That evening people brought many who were demon-possessed, and Jesus cast out the spirits with a word and healed everyone who was sick. His authority over evil and sickness was complete and effortless.
entries.8:17: This happened to fulfill what the prophet Isaiah had said about the servant who took up our pains and diseases. Jesus' healing shows he came to carry the burdens that weigh people down.
entries.8:18: Seeing the large crowd around him, Jesus told his disciples to cross to the other side of the lake. He was not controlled by the crowd but moved on to where he was needed next.
entries.8:19: A teacher of the law came and promised to follow Jesus wherever he went. He was enthusiastic, but Jesus would test what that commitment really meant.
entries.8:20: Jesus replied that foxes have dens and birds have nests, but he had no home of his own. Following him may mean giving up comfort and security rather than gaining them.
entries.8:21: Another disciple asked to first go and bury his father before following Jesus. Family duties can be good, but they can also become a reason to delay following him.
entries.8:22: Jesus told him to follow now and let the spiritually dead handle burial matters. Following Jesus takes priority over even the strongest family obligations.
entries.8:23: Jesus got into a boat, and his disciples went with him. They stayed close to him, which set the stage for what happened next.
entries.8:24: A violent storm hit the lake and waves swept over the boat, but Jesus was asleep. The storm was real and dangerous, yet Jesus was at peace.
entries.8:25: The disciples woke him and cried out for help, fearing they would die. In their panic they turned to Jesus, which was the right place to turn.
entries.8:26: Jesus asked why they were afraid and pointed out their small faith, then he commanded the winds and sea and everything became calm. Fear and faith can coexist, but his word brings peace.
entries.8:27: The men were amazed and asked what kind of man this was, since even wind and sea obeyed him. They were beginning to see that Jesus was far more than an ordinary teacher.
entries.8:28: On the other side, in the region of the Gadarenes, two violent men with evil spirits came out from the tombs and met him. No one could pass that way because of them, yet they came out to face Jesus.
entries.8:29: The spirits cried out, asking what Jesus wanted with them and whether he had come to punish them before the appointed time. Even evil powers recognized who Jesus was and feared his authority.
entries.8:30: A large herd of pigs was feeding some distance away. This detail sets up what happens next and shows the setting was a Gentile region.
entries.8:31: The evil spirits begged Jesus to send them into the herd of pigs if he was going to drive them out. They had to ask permission and could not act on their own.
entries.8:32: Jesus told them to go, and the spirits entered the pigs, which rushed down a steep bank into the sea and drowned. Jesus' word freed the men, though it cost the herd.
entries.8:33: The men tending the pigs ran off to town and reported everything, including what had happened to the two men. News of Jesus' power spread, but not everyone would welcome it.
entries.8:34: The whole town came out to meet Jesus and begged him to leave their region. They were more unsettled by the loss of their pigs than moved by the rescue of two men.
entries.9:1: Jesus crossed the lake by boat and came back to his own home town. It shows he moved around to keep teaching and helping people.
entries.9:2: Friends brought a paralyzed man to Jesus, and Jesus saw their faith and told the man his sins were forgiven. It means Jesus cares about what is wrong inside us, not just our bodies.
entries.9:3: The religious teachers thought Jesus was insulting God by claiming to forgive sins. They did not yet understand who he really was.
entries.9:4: Jesus knew what they were thinking and asked why their thoughts were so hostile. Nothing we think is hidden from him.
entries.9:5: Jesus asked which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk. Saying either is easy; doing either takes real power.
entries.9:6: Jesus proved he had God's authority to forgive sins by healing the man right there. He backed up his words with an action everyone could see.
entries.9:7: The man got up and walked home, just as Jesus told him. The healing was immediate and complete.
entries.9:8: The crowd was awed and praised God for giving such authority to a human being. Seeing Jesus at work should move us to worship God too.
entries.9:9: Jesus called a tax collector named Matthew to follow him, and he got up and did it at once. Jesus reaches out to people others look down on.
entries.9:10: Jesus ate at Matthew's house with tax collectors and other outcasts. He was willing to be close to people with bad reputations.
entries.9:11: The Pharisees criticized Jesus for eating with such people. They judged by reputation rather than by need.
entries.9:12: Jesus answered that sick people need a doctor, not healthy ones. He came for those who know they need help, not those who think they are fine.
entries.9:13: Jesus told them to learn that God wants mercy more than ritual, and that he came for sinners, not the self-righteous. God values compassion over outward religion.
entries.9:14: John's followers asked why Jesus' disciples did not fast like they and the Pharisees did. They were comparing religious practices.
entries.9:15: Jesus said his friends don't mourn while he is with them, but a time will come when he is taken away and then they will fast. There is a right time for sorrow and a right time for joy.
entries.9:16: No one patches an old coat with new cloth, because it tears away and makes the hole worse. New and old ways don't always mix well.
entries.9:17: New wine must go in new wineskins or both are ruined. Jesus' new way of doing things needs fresh containers, not worn-out ones.
entries.9:18: A leader came and knelt before Jesus, begging him to come and bring his dead daughter back to life. He believed Jesus could do the impossible.
entries.9:19: Jesus got up and went with him, and his disciples followed. Jesus responds when people come to him in desperate faith.
entries.9:20: A woman who had been bleeding for twelve years came up behind Jesus and touched the edge of his robe. She was desperate and hoped for healing.
entries.9:21: She told herself that just touching his clothes would heal her. Her faith was small and quiet, but real.
entries.9:22: Jesus turned, called her daughter, and told her that her faith had healed her, and she was well from that moment. Jesus notices quiet faith and responds to it.
entries.9:23: At the leader's house Jesus saw flute players and a noisy crowd. It was the usual mourning scene for a death.
entries.9:24: Jesus said the girl was only sleeping, and the crowd laughed at him. People often mock what they don't understand.
entries.9:25: After sending the crowd out, Jesus took the girl's hand and she got up. He brought life where there had been death.
entries.9:26: News of this spread through the whole region. People could not keep quiet about what Jesus did.
entries.9:27: Two blind men followed Jesus, shouting for mercy and calling him the Son of David. They recognized who he was and begged for help.
entries.9:28: When they came inside, Jesus asked if they believed he could do it, and they said yes. Faith is the key he looks for.
entries.9:29: Jesus touched their eyes and said it would be done according to their faith. He honors the trust people put in him.
entries.9:30: Their eyes were opened, and Jesus warned them firmly not to tell anyone. He did not want to be known only as a miracle worker.
entries.9:31: But they went out and spread the news everywhere anyway. People often can't help talking about what Jesus has done for them.
entries.9:32: A man who could not speak and was controlled by an evil spirit was brought to Jesus. He was in serious need of help.
entries.9:33: When the evil spirit left, the man could speak, and the crowd was amazed, saying nothing like this had ever been seen in Israel. Jesus' power was unlike anything they knew.
entries.9:34: The Pharisees claimed Jesus drove out evil spirits by the power of the prince of evil spirits. They refused to accept the plain evidence and twisted it.
entries.9:35: Jesus traveled through towns and villages, teaching, preaching the good news, and healing every kind of sickness. He cared for people's whole lives, not just their souls.
entries.9:36: When Jesus saw the crowds, he felt deep compassion because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep with no shepherd. He sees people's need and feels for them.
entries.9:37: Jesus told his disciples the harvest is large but the workers are few. There is plenty of work to do and not enough people doing it.
entries.9:38: He told them to pray that the Lord of the harvest would send out workers. We should ask God to raise up people to care for those in need.
entries.10:1: Jesus gathered his twelve closest followers and gave them real authority to cast out evil spirits and heal every kind of sickness and pain. This means the work he sends people to do comes with power from him, not from themselves.
entries.10:2: Matthew begins listing the twelve men Jesus chose, starting with Simon Peter and his brother Andrew, then James and John, the sons of Zebedee. These were ordinary men whom Jesus picked by name for a special task.
entries.10:3: The list continues with Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, and Matthew, who had worked collecting taxes for Rome. It shows Jesus chose a mixed group, including people others looked down on.
entries.10:4: The list ends with Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot, the one who would later betray Jesus. Even among Jesus' chosen twelve, one turned against him.
entries.10:5: Jesus sent the twelve out with clear instructions not to go to non-Jewish people or into Samaritan towns. He gave them a specific starting place for their mission.
entries.10:6: Instead, they were to go to the people of Israel who had wandered away from God, like lost sheep. Their first job was to bring God's own people back to him.
entries.10:7: As they traveled, they were to announce that God's kingdom was near. The message was simple: God's rule is coming close to people now.
entries.10:8: They were to heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, and drive out evil spirits, giving freely because they had received freely. What they had been given as a gift was to be passed on as a gift, not sold.
entries.10:9: They were not to take gold, silver, or copper money with them. They were to travel depending on God and on the hospitality of the people they served.
entries.10:10: They were not to carry extra bags, clothes, shoes, or a walking stick, because a worker deserves to be fed by those he serves. Those who do the work should be supported by the people who benefit from it.
entries.10:11: In each town they were to look for a respected person and stay in that person's home until they left the area. Staying in one place showed they were not shopping around for better lodging.
entries.10:12: When they entered a house, they were to greet it with a blessing of peace. Their arrival was meant to bring something good to that home.
entries.10:13: If the household welcomed them, that peace would rest on it; if not, the blessing would return to them. A welcome or a rejection does not cancel the good they came to bring.
entries.10:14: If a house or town refused to receive them or listen to their words, they were to shake its dust off their feet as they left. This was a visible sign that they were done with that place and not responsible for its response.
entries.10:15: Jesus said that on judgment day it will be easier for Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town. Rejecting the message brought to them directly is a serious matter.
entries.10:16: Jesus sent them out like sheep among wolves, so they needed to be as wise as snakes and as gentle as doves. They were to be careful and smart without becoming harsh or harmful.
entries.10:17: They were to watch out for people, because they would be handed over to councils and beaten in synagogues. Following Jesus would bring real opposition, even from religious settings.
entries.10:18: They would be brought before governors and kings because of Jesus, to testify to them and to non-Jews. Even being put on trial would become a chance to tell others about him.
entries.10:19: When they were arrested, they were not to worry about what to say or how to say it, because the right words would be given to them at that moment. They could trust God to supply what they needed when the time came.
entries.10:20: The words they spoke in those moments would not really be their own, but the Spirit of their Father speaking through them. God himself would speak on their behalf.
entries.10:21: Brothers would hand brothers over to death, fathers their children, and children would turn against their parents and cause them to be killed. Faith in Jesus would split even the closest family ties.
entries.10:22: They would be hated by everyone because of Jesus' name, but the one who stays strong to the end will be saved. Being disliked is not the end of the story; endurance is what matters.
entries.10:23: When people were cruel to them in one town, they were to flee to another, because they would not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes. There was no shame in escaping danger; the mission would still be completed in God's time.
entries.10:24: A student is not above his teacher, and a servant is not above his master. Followers of Jesus should not expect better treatment than he received.
entries.10:25: It is enough for a student to be like his teacher and a servant like his master; if people called the head of the house Beelzebub, they will say worse about his household. If they insulted Jesus, his followers should expect the same.
entries.10:26: They were not to be afraid of those people, because nothing hidden will stay hidden and nothing secret will stay secret. The truth about who is right will eventually come out.
entries.10:27: What Jesus told them privately, they were to speak openly, and what they heard in secret, they were to announce from the rooftops. His teaching was not meant to stay quiet.
entries.10:28: They were not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul; instead, they should fear the one who has power to destroy both soul and body in hell. Physical death is not the worst thing that can happen.
entries.10:29: Two sparrows are sold for a tiny coin, yet not one of them dies without your Father knowing. God notices even the smallest, cheapest creatures.
entries.10:30: Even the hairs on your head are all counted. God knows you in far more detail than you know yourself.
entries.10:31: So they should not be afraid, because they are worth more than a whole flock of sparrows. If God cares for small birds, he surely cares for people.
entries.10:32: Everyone who openly acknowledges Jesus before people, he will acknowledge before his Father in heaven. Standing with Jesus publicly matters, and he will stand with those who do.
entries.10:33: But anyone who denies knowing Jesus before people, he will deny before his Father in heaven. Turning your back on him has real consequences.
entries.10:34: Jesus said not to think he came to bring peace on earth; he came not to bring peace but a sword. Following him would cause sharp division, not comfortable harmony everywhere.
entries.10:35: He came to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Loyalty to Jesus can create conflict even inside a family.
entries.10:36: A person's enemies will be members of his own household. The people closest to you may be the ones who oppose you most.
entries.10:37: Anyone who loves father or mother, son or daughter more than Jesus is not fit for him. Jesus must come first, even ahead of the dearest family relationships.
entries.10:38: Anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Jesus is not fit for him. Following Jesus means accepting hardship and putting your own life on the line for him.
entries.10:39: Whoever tries to hold on to his life will lose it, and whoever gives up his life for Jesus will find it. Clinging to your own comfort costs you what matters most, while surrendering it to Jesus gains it back.
entries.10:40: Whoever welcomes you welcomes Jesus, and whoever welcomes Jesus welcomes the one who sent him. How people treat Jesus' followers is how they treat Jesus and God himself.
entries.10:41: Welcoming and supporting someone because they speak for God or live rightly means you share in the good that comes to them. Even small acts of respect toward faithful people count with God.
entries.10:42: Even a simple kindness to someone overlooked and unimportant, done because they belong to Jesus, will not be forgotten by God. No act of care is too small to matter.
entries.11:1: After Jesus finished instructing his twelve disciples, he left and began teaching and preaching in the towns around there. This shows Jesus kept working steadily, and it reminds the reader that his mission didn't stop with one speech.
entries.11:2: John the Baptist, now in prison, heard about the things Christ was doing and sent his own disciples to ask him about it. Even a faithful man like John had questions when life got hard, so the reader need not feel ashamed of doubt.
entries.11:3: John's disciples asked Jesus directly whether he was the promised one or whether they should keep waiting for someone else. It's an honest question about who Jesus really is, and every reader has to face that same question.
entries.11:4: Jesus didn't argue; he told them to go back and report to John what they were actually seeing and hearing. He let his actions answer the question, and the reader is invited to look at what Jesus does, not just what people say about him.
entries.11:5: Jesus listed the concrete things happening: blind people seeing, lame people walking, lepers healed, deaf people hearing, dead people raised, and good news given to the poor. These are real signs that God's promised rescue was arriving, and they show the reader that Jesus cared about people's actual suffering.
entries.11:6: Jesus said a person is blessed who doesn't stumble or give up on him. It's a gentle warning that doubts and disappointments can trip us up, and it encourages the reader to keep trusting Jesus even when things are confusing.
entries.11:7: As John's messengers left, Jesus asked the crowd what they had gone out into the wilderness to see—surely not just a reed swaying in the wind. He was saying John was no flimsy, unimportant figure, so the reader should take John's role seriously.
entries.11:8: Jesus asked if they went out to see a man dressed in fancy clothes, then pointed out that such people live in palaces, not deserts. John was clearly not a soft, comfortable courtier, and the reader learns that God's messengers are often rough and plain rather than polished.
entries.11:9: Jesus asked if they went out to see a prophet, and answered yes—but one even greater than a prophet. John had a bigger role than the prophets before him, and the reader should recognize how significant his place in the story is.
entries.11:10: Jesus quoted Scripture showing that John was the messenger sent ahead to prepare the way for him. This means John's work wasn't random; it was planned by God long before, and it points the reader straight to Jesus.
entries.11:11: Jesus said no one born of women was greater than John, yet even the least person in God's kingdom is greater than he. This is a striking statement that those who belong to Jesus' kingdom have a position and closeness to God that even John, great as he was, did not yet enjoy.
entries.11:12: Jesus said that from John's time until now the kingdom of heaven is pressing forward, and forceful people are seizing it. It pictures God's rule as something powerful and advancing that people respond to with real energy, and it challenges the reader not to be passive about it.
entries.11:13: Jesus explained that all the prophets and the law spoke until John—meaning the old era of preparation reached its climax with him. John stands at the turning point, and the reader is meant to see that a new stage in God's plan has begun.
entries.11:14: Jesus said that if they were willing to accept it, John was the Elijah who was expected to come. This identifies John as the promised forerunner, and it asks the reader to accept Jesus' own explanation of what God was doing.
entries.11:15: Jesus said that whoever has ears should listen. It's a plain call to pay attention to what he just said, and it reminds the reader that hearing without really listening misses the point.
entries.11:16: Jesus compared his generation to children sitting in the marketplace calling out to each other. He was pointing out how people were acting childish and contrary, and the reader is warned against that same stubbornness.
entries.11:17: The children complained that they played happy music and nobody danced, then played sad music and nobody mourned. Jesus was saying the people rejected both joyful and solemn messengers, and the reader should watch for that tendency to find fault no matter what.
entries.11:18: John came not eating or drinking, and people said he had an evil spirit. Jesus shows how people twist even a strict, self-denying life into a reason to reject the messenger, and the reader learns that critics will always find something to complain about.
entries.11:19: Jesus came eating and drinking, and people called him a glutton, a drunk, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Yet Jesus said wisdom is proven right by what it produces, so the reader should judge by results rather than by gossip.
entries.11:20: Jesus began to speak sternly to the towns where he had done most of his miracles, because they hadn't turned from their sins. Great privilege brings great responsibility, and the reader is reminded that seeing God's work should lead to real change, not just amazement.
entries.11:21: Jesus pronounced woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida, saying that if the same miracles had been done in wicked Tyre and Sidon, those cities would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. It shows that people who had the most evidence were the least responsive, and it warns the reader not to presume on God's patience.
entries.11:22: Jesus said it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on judgment day than for those towns. This means God's judgment takes into account what people were given, and the reader should take seriously the light they've received.
entries.11:23: Jesus addressed Capernaum, which had been lifted high with privilege, and said it would be brought down to the grave; if Sodom had seen such miracles, it would have survived. The reader learns that closeness to Jesus and his works is no guarantee if there's no repentance.
entries.11:24: Jesus said it will be more bearable for Sodom on judgment day than for Capernaum. Even the notoriously wicked city will fare better than a town that saw Jesus' miracles and ignored them, which is a sober warning to the reader.
entries.11:25: Jesus thanked the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, for hiding these things from the wise and learned and revealing them to little children. God's truth isn't grasped by pride or cleverness but by humble, childlike openness, and the reader is invited to come that way.
entries.11:26: Jesus added that this was what pleased the Father. It shows Jesus fully agreeing with God's way of doing things, and it reassures the reader that God's choices are good even when they seem upside down.
entries.11:27: Jesus said the Father has handed everything over to him, and that no one truly knows the Son except the Father, or the Father except the Son and those the Son reveals him to. This means knowing God comes through Jesus, and the reader is pointed to him as the only real way in.
entries.11:28: Jesus invites the tired to come, not to try harder. Rest is something he gives.
entries.11:29: Jesus invited people to take his yoke on themselves and learn from him, because he is gentle and humble, and promised rest for their souls. A yoke is a burden harness, so he's saying life with him is a shared load, and the weary reader is offered real rest rather than more pressure.
entries.11:30: Jesus said his yoke is good and the weight he gives is not hard. Following him still involves work, but it's a kind, bearable load rather than a crushing one, and the reader can trust that Jesus won't overload them.
entries.12:1: Jesus and his disciples were walking through grain fields on the Sabbath and the disciples picked some grain to eat because they were hungry. It shows that real human need matters, even on a day set aside for rest.
entries.12:2: The Pharisees accused the disciples of breaking the Sabbath rules by doing this. They were quick to judge others over rules rather than care about people's hunger.
entries.12:3: Jesus answers them with a question about David, reminding them of a story they should already know. He is pointing out that their strict rules don't cover every situation.
entries.12:4: David and his men ate bread from God's house that was only allowed for priests, and God did not condemn him. This shows that need can outweigh ritual rules.
entries.12:5: Jesus notes that priests work in the Temple on the Sabbath and are not considered guilty. So the Sabbath rules were never meant to be absolute in every case.
entries.12:6: Jesus says something greater than the Temple is here, meaning himself. If the Temple allowed exceptions, then his presence allows even more.
entries.12:7: God cares more about mercy than about religious rituals, and if the Pharisees understood this they would not have condemned innocent people. Readers are reminded to show mercy rather than nitpick.
entries.12:8: Jesus claims authority over the Sabbath as the Son of Man. He, not human tradition, decides what the Sabbath really means.
entries.12:9: Jesus left that place and went into the local synagogue. He continued to teach and worship in the usual gathering place.
entries.12:10: A man with a withered hand was there, and the Pharisees asked Jesus whether healing on the Sabbath was allowed, hoping to trap him. They were using a suffering man as a test case.
entries.12:11: Jesus points out that any of them would rescue a sheep that fell into a pit on the Sabbath. They already made exceptions when their own interests were at stake.
entries.12:12: Since a person is worth far more than a sheep, doing good for someone on the Sabbath is clearly right. Kindness to people should never be put on hold.
entries.12:13: Jesus told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was healed completely. The man's simple obedience led to his restoration.
entries.12:14: The Pharisees left and plotted how to kill Jesus. Their concern for rules had hardened into murderous hatred.
entries.12:15: Jesus knew their plans and withdrew, and large crowds followed him, and he healed them all. He did not stop caring for people even when threatened.
entries.12:16: Jesus told the people he healed not to publicize him. He did not want his mission reduced to a spectacle.
entries.12:17: This happened to fulfill what the prophet Isaiah had spoken long before. God's plans were being worked out exactly as promised.
entries.12:18: God calls Jesus his chosen servant whom he loves and is pleased with, and he gives him his Spirit to bring justice to the nations. This identifies Jesus as God's specially chosen one.
entries.12:19: He will not quarrel or shout or make a public scene. His way is quiet and humble rather than loud and aggressive.
entries.12:20: He will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a faintly burning wick until justice wins. He is gentle with the weak and will not give up on them.
entries.12:21: The nations will put their hope in his name. People from every background can trust him.
entries.12:22: They brought Jesus a man who was blind, mute, and oppressed by an evil spirit, and Jesus healed him so he could see and speak. No condition is beyond his help.
entries.12:23: The crowds were amazed and wondered if Jesus was the promised Son of David, the Messiah. People recognized something extraordinary in him.
entries.12:24: The Pharisees claimed Jesus drove out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Instead of accepting the obvious good, they twisted it into an accusation.
entries.12:25: Jesus knew their thoughts and said that any kingdom or household divided against itself will fall apart. Internal conflict destroys whatever it touches.
entries.12:26: If Satan were casting out Satan, he would be fighting himself and his kingdom could not stand. Their accusation makes no sense.
entries.12:27: If Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebub, then by what power do their own followers cast them out? Their own practice exposes the inconsistency of their charge.
entries.12:28: If Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, then God's kingdom has truly arrived among them. The healing power shows God is at work.
entries.12:29: No one can rob a strong man's house without first tying him up, and only then can his goods be taken. Jesus is saying he has bound the strong enemy and is setting people free.
entries.12:30: Anyone who is not with Jesus is against him, and anyone who does not gather with him scatters. There is no neutral ground when it comes to him.
entries.12:31: Every sin and insult against God can be forgiven, but speaking evil against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. This is a serious warning about hardening your heart against God's clear work.
entries.12:32: Words against Jesus can be forgiven, but words against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven in this life or the next. Rejecting God's Spirit persistently is the most dangerous thing a person can do.
entries.12:33: A tree is known by its fruit, so make the tree good and its fruit will be good. What you produce shows what you really are.
entries.12:34: Jesus calls them a brood of snakes and says that evil people cannot speak good things, because the mouth speaks from what fills the heart. Your words reveal what is inside you.
entries.12:35: A good person brings good things out of the good stored in them, and an evil person brings out evil. What you treasure inside eventually comes out in your words and actions.
entries.12:36: Jesus says people will give an account on judgment day for every careless word they have spoken. Words matter more than we often think.
entries.12:37: Your words will show whether you are in the right, and your words will be used to judge you. What you say has real consequences.
entries.12:38: Some religious leaders asked Jesus for a sign to prove his authority. They wanted more evidence even after all they had seen.
entries.12:39: Jesus called them an evil and unfaithful generation and said the only sign they would get was the sign of Jonah. He refused to perform on demand for people who would not believe.
entries.12:40: Just as Jonah was in the belly of the great fish for three days and nights, Jesus would be in the heart of the earth for three days and nights. This points ahead to his death and resurrection.
entries.12:41: The people of Nineveh turned from their sins when Jonah preached, so on judgment day they will stand as a witness against Jesus' generation that ignored someone greater than Jonah. For the reader, it means hearing God's message and actually changing matters more than who delivers it.
entries.12:42: The queen of Sheba traveled far just to hear Solomon's wisdom, so she will stand as a witness against those who had someone greater than Solomon right in front of them and paid no attention. For the reader, it warns against ignoring the wisdom God offers close at hand.
entries.12:43: An evil spirit that leaves a person wanders through dry, empty places looking for a place to rest but finds none. For the reader, it pictures a life that is cleared of wrong but not filled with anything good.
entries.12:44: The spirit decides to return to the person it left and finds the life swept clean and tidy but empty. For the reader, it shows that simply removing bad habits without filling the space with God leaves room for worse.
entries.12:45: The spirit brings seven spirits worse than itself, and they settle in, so the person ends up worse off than before; Jesus says the same will happen to his generation. For the reader, it means cleaning up your life without turning to God can leave you in a worse place.
entries.12:46: While Jesus was still speaking to the crowd, his mother and brothers arrived and wanted to talk with him. For the reader, it shows that even family can interrupt, and Jesus had to decide what mattered most.
entries.12:47: Someone told Jesus that his mother and brothers were outside waiting to speak with him. For the reader, it sets up Jesus' surprising answer about who really counts as family.
entries.12:48: Jesus answered the messenger by asking who his mother and brothers really are. For the reader, it signals that he is about to redefine family in a way that goes beyond blood relations.
entries.12:49: Jesus gestured toward his disciples and said they were his mother and brothers. For the reader, it shows that following him creates a real family bond with others who follow him too.
entries.12:50: Jesus said that anyone who does what his Father in heaven wants is his brother, sister, and mother. For the reader, it means belonging to Jesus is based on doing God's will, not on family background.
entries.13:1: Jesus left the house and sat down by the edge of the sea. It shows him teaching in ordinary, everyday places where people could easily come to him.
entries.13:2: So many people gathered that Jesus got into a boat while the crowd stood on the shore. He used the boat as a natural platform so everyone could hear him.
entries.13:3: Jesus taught the crowd using a story about a farmer scattering seed. He often used familiar everyday pictures to explain deeper truths about God.
entries.13:4: Some seed fell on the path where the ground was hard, and birds quickly ate it. This pictures how some teaching is snatched away before it can take root.
entries.13:5: Some seed landed on rocky ground with little soil, so it sprouted fast. Quick growth can look promising but may not last without depth.
entries.13:6: When the sun grew hot, the shallow-rooted plant dried up and died. Anything that starts without real roots will not survive hard times.
entries.13:7: Some seed fell among thorny weeds that grew up and choked it. Good things can be crowded out by other concerns that compete for our attention.
entries.13:8: Other seed fell on good soil and produced a crop, some a hundred, some sixty, some thirty times what was planted. When teaching is received well, it can produce far more than seems possible.
entries.13:9: Jesus urged anyone willing to listen to really pay attention. He is asking the hearer to take his words seriously, not just hear them casually.
entries.13:10: The disciples asked Jesus why he taught the crowds in stories. They wanted to understand his method and why he didn't speak more directly.
entries.13:11: Jesus said his close followers were given insight into God's kingdom secrets, but others were not. Understanding spiritual things is a gift that grows as people respond.
entries.13:12: Those who use what they have been given will receive more, but those who neglect it will lose even that. Responding to what we learn matters greatly.
entries.13:13: Jesus used stories because many people looked and listened without really grasping the meaning. The stories revealed truth to some and left others unmoved.
entries.13:14: This fulfilled Isaiah's words about people who hear and see but never understand. It warns that it is possible to be near the truth and still miss it.
entries.13:15: The people's hearts had grown dull, their ears slow, and their eyes closed, so they would not turn to God and be healed. This is a serious warning about hardening yourself against God over time.
entries.13:16: Jesus called his disciples blessed because their eyes and ears were open to what he was doing. Being able to see and hear spiritual truth is a real privilege.
entries.13:17: Many prophets and good people longed to see and hear what the disciples were experiencing but never did. We should value the truth we have been given.
entries.13:18: Jesus began to explain the story of the farmer sowing seed. He wanted his disciples to understand what it meant, not just enjoy the picture.
entries.13:19: The seed on the path is someone who hears the kingdom message but doesn't understand it, and the Evil One quickly takes it away. Truth that is never taken to heart can be lost almost immediately.
entries.13:20: The seed on rocky ground is someone who hears the message and receives it with immediate joy. An enthusiastic start is good, but it is not the same as deep commitment.
entries.13:21: This person has no root and lasts only a while, falling away when trouble or hardship comes because of the message. Faith that is only surface-deep will not stand up under pressure.
entries.13:22: The seed among thorns is someone whose faith is choked by worries about life and the lure of wealth, so it bears no fruit. Cares and money can quietly crowd out what God is doing in us.
entries.13:23: The seed on good soil is someone who hears the message, understands it, and produces a crop many times over. Listening with understanding leads to real, lasting results.
entries.13:24: Jesus told another story comparing God's kingdom to a man who planted good seed in his field. He is describing how God's work begins with something good.
entries.13:25: While everyone slept, an enemy came and planted weeds among the wheat, then slipped away. Bad things can be sown into good situations quietly and unexpectedly.
entries.13:26: When the plants grew and formed grain, the weeds showed up too. Problems often become visible only once things start to grow.
entries.13:27: The servants asked the owner how weeds could appear in a field where he had planted good seed. It is natural to wonder why evil shows up where God has done good.
entries.13:28: The owner said an enemy had done it, and the servants offered to pull up the weeds. The owner knew the source of the problem and was ready to deal with it.
entries.13:29: The owner said no, because pulling the weeds might uproot the wheat along with them. Sometimes rushing to remove what seems wrong can harm what is good.
entries.13:30: He told them to let both grow until harvest, then the weeds would be burned and the wheat stored. God will sort things out at the right time, and we can trust his timing.
entries.13:31: Jesus compared God's kingdom to a mustard seed that a man planted in his field. He is showing that God's work often starts very small.
entries.13:32: Though it is the smallest of seeds, it grows into a large plant where birds can rest. Small beginnings under God's care can become something big and life-giving.
entries.13:33: Jesus compared God's kingdom to yeast that a woman mixed into dough until it spread through all of it. God's influence works quietly but changes everything it touches.
entries.13:34: Jesus taught the crowds entirely in stories and said nothing to them without a story. He chose this way to communicate truth to ordinary people.
entries.13:35: This fulfilled what the prophet said about opening his mouth in stories and revealing things hidden since the beginning. Jesus was revealing long-hidden truths in a way people could grasp.
entries.13:36: Jesus left the crowd and went into the house, and his disciples asked him to explain the story about the weeds. They wanted to understand what he had taught.
entries.13:37: Jesus said the one who plants the good seed is the Son of Man, meaning himself. He is the one who brings God's good message into the world.
entries.13:38: The field is the world, the good seed are the people of God's kingdom, and the weeds are the people of the Evil One. The world contains both, and they grow side by side.
entries.13:39: The enemy who planted the weeds is Satan, the harvest is the end of the world, and the harvesters are angels. There will be a final time when God sets everything right.
entries.13:40: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned, so it will be at the end of the world. This is a sober reminder that evil will not go on forever and God will judge it.
entries.13:41: Jesus says that at the end, his angels will remove from his kingdom everything that causes people to sin and everyone who does evil. This means evil will not be tolerated forever, and we should take our own wrongdoing seriously.
entries.13:42: Those removed will be thrown into fire, where there is great sadness and pain. This is a serious warning that rejecting God has real and painful consequences.
entries.13:43: Then good people will shine brightly like the sun in their Father's kingdom. This gives hope that those who live rightly will be honored and joyful in the end, so it is worth listening carefully.
entries.13:44: God's kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field; a man finds it and joyfully sells everything to buy that field. This means the kingdom is worth more than anything else, and giving up everything for it brings real joy.
entries.13:45: God's kingdom is also like a merchant looking for fine pearls. This shows that the kingdom is something valuable worth actively searching for.
entries.13:46: When the merchant finds one pearl of great value, he sells everything he has to buy it. This means the kingdom is worth more than all our possessions, and we should be willing to give up anything for it.
entries.13:47: God's kingdom is like a net thrown into the sea that catches fish of every kind. This means the kingdom gathers all sorts of people, good and bad mixed together for now.
entries.13:48: When the net is full, the fishermen sit down and keep the good fish but throw away the bad. This means a time is coming when good and bad will be separated.
entries.13:49: Jesus says this is how it will be at the end of the world: angels will separate the bad from the good. This reminds us that God will finally judge everyone fairly.
